source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems
finding: Founding Bayesian arbitration model. A tree-search (planning) controller and a cached TD controller each track their own uncertainty. The one that is more certain about value controls choice. Early in training the tree system wins, later the cache wins. It reproduces devaluation insensitivity after extended training.
numbers: Simulation account of rodent devaluation data; no new human numbers.
quote: each controller is deployed when it should be most accurate
limits: Arbitration was by uncertainty only. Cost of thinking (time, effort) was not in the model. Later work (Keramati 2011) added it. Predictions about which system is uncertain were not tested directly in humans.
agent_relevance: S0 gate can be read as: plan when the cache is uncertain. But uncertainty alone ignores cost, so it is half a gate.

source: Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, Dolan (2011) Model-based influences on humans' choices and striatal prediction errors
finding: The two-step task. First choice leads to one of two second-stage states with 70/30 transition. Pure model-free predicts stay after reward regardless of transition. Pure model-based predicts a cross-over. Humans show both. Ventral striatal prediction errors also reflect model-based values, not pure model-free.
numbers: N=17 fMRI participants. Common transition 70%, rare 30%. Reward probabilities drift as Gaussian random walks. Hybrid model weight w (0=free, 1=based) fit per person; median w about 0.39 as re-tabulated by Feher da Silva and Hare.
limits: Small N. Mixture weight is only identified if the task model assumed by the analyst equals the participant's model (see b09, b10). No comprehension check on instructions.
agent_relevance: The task gives a clean behavioural test of whether an agent uses a model of consequences or only repeats what paid before. Usable as a probe, not as a loop design.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli, Piray (2011) Speed/accuracy trade-off between the habitual and the goal-directed processes
finding: Arbitration by cost. Planning gives accurate value but takes time. The cache is fast but can be wrong. The model plans only when the value of information from deliberating exceeds the cost of delay, where cost = deliberation time x average reward rate. Explains early outcome sensitivity and late insensitivity, and reaction time falling with training and rising with number of choices.
numbers: Simulations of devaluation, concurrent-choice and reversal-learning RT data (Pessiglione reversal task: RT high while searching, low once the rule applied). Cost of deliberation = average reward rate x deliberation time.
quote: arbitration between the two processes that makes an approximately optimal balance between search-time and accuracy
limits: Model fits published data; no new human experiment in this paper. Assumes value of information is computable, which is the hard part. Tonic dopamine as reward-rate signal is a prediction, not shown here.
agent_relevance: Closest formal match to the S0 gate: plan iff expected gain of planning exceeds its cost, with cost rising when time is valuable.

source: Keramati, Smittenaar, Dolan, Dayan (2016) Adaptive integration of habits into depth-limited planning defines a habitual-goal-directed spectrum
finding: Three-step task. Humans do not switch between full planning and pure habit. They plan a few steps and then plug in cached values (plan-until-habit). A 700 ms time limit made planning shallower and plug-in use stronger.
numbers: Planning effect stronger in the high-resource than low-resource group after rewarded (P=0.011) and unrewarded (P=0.027) trials. Plan-until-habit effect stronger under time pressure after rewarded trials. Small lab sample (thirty-odd).
limits: Mixed-effects lagged regression agreed. Single study; no large replication found in this search.
agent_relevance: Better than a binary gate: the agent can search to a depth then use a cheap cached estimate. Depth, not on/off, is the control variable.

source: Sezener, Dezfouli, Keramati (2019) Optimizing the depth and direction of prospective planning using information values
finding: Extends b03/b04. Computes the benefit of expanding one more step in a given direction and compares it with the time cost. Explains time-pressure effect on depth, reward-magnitude effect on direction, and slow shift to habit with training.
numbers: Grid-world simulations; qualitative fits to earlier human and animal results.
limits: Simulation paper. Value-of-information computation needs a model of the cache's error, which an LLM does not have without a probe.
agent_relevance: Gives a stopping rule for search: stop when the expected gain of one more expansion is below its cost.

source: Kool, Cushman, Gershman (2016) When does model-based control pay off?
finding: Key challenge to the arbitration story. In the standard two-step task and variants, model-based control earns almost no more reward than model-free, across the whole range of learning parameters. So there is no accuracy-versus-effort trade-off for humans to arbitrate. Five task factors cancel the benefit. A redesigned task restores a measurable benefit, and humans then rely more on model-based control.
numbers: Redesigned task: 199 online participants, 125 trials. Simulations over the full learning-rate and weight grid; the original task showed no reward gain from higher w.
limits: Online sample. Redesigned task changes several things at once. Concerns benefit of planning, not neural implementation.
agent_relevance: Lesson for the S0 gate: planning has to be shown to pay on this task class before it is switched on. If the cache is nearly as good, planning is waste.

source: Kool, Gershman, Cushman (2017) Cost-benefit arbitration between multiple reinforcement-learning systems
finding: Follow-up to b06 (known from search metadata only, not read). People raised model-based use when the payoff difference between systems was larger, in line with a cost-benefit rule.
numbers: Not recorded; paper not opened.
limits: Not opened. Verify before citing numbers.
agent_relevance: Supports a payoff-sensitive gate in humans.

source: Patzelt, Kool, Millner, Gershman (2019) Incentives boost model-based control across a range of severity on several psychiatric constructs
finding: Large replication of the incentive effect. Higher stakes on a trial raised model-based weight. Greater average reward rate also predicted more model-based control, replicating Kool and colleagues.
numbers: N=839 online. Paired t(838)=10.21, p<.001, Cohen d=0.35 (high vs low stakes). Bayesian slope of reward rate on model-based control: low stakes beta mean 0.473 [0.417, 0.526]; high stakes 0.357 [0.290, 0.404].
limits: Online sample, self-reported psychiatric status. Effect is moderate. Incentive effect does not prove the mechanism is cost-benefit rather than motivation.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the planning gate moves with payoff: raising stakes lifts planning share by about a third of a standard deviation.

source: Feher da Silva & Hare (2020) Humans primarily use model-based inference in the two-stage task
finding: Failed replication of the hybrid result. With story-based instructions and a comprehension quiz, participants became mostly model-based with little simple model-free influence. A model-based agent with a wrong task model looks like a hybrid under the standard analysis.
numbers: Median model-based weight: Daw 2011 (N=17) 0.39; Kool 2016 re-analysis (N=206) 0.24; spaceship (N=21) 0.78; magic carpet (N=24) 0.79. Simulated purely model-based agents with correct model: median w 0.94 (95% range 0.74 to 1.00); with an 'unlucky symbol' wrong model: median w 0.36 (0.24 to 0.48).
quote: more detailed task instructions lead participants to make primarily model-based choices
limits: Small new samples (21 and 24). Does not show model-free learning is absent everywhere. Preprint text plus published abstract opened.
agent_relevance: A mixed score may be instruction misunderstanding, not two systems. For an LLM, prompt wording may do the same, so any arbitration test must check task comprehension.

source: Akam, Costa, Dayan (2015) Simple plans or sophisticated habits? State, transition and learning interactions in the two-step task
finding: Simulation work showing some model-free strategies masquerade as model-based. Small changes to the task create correlations between action value and later events, so the consecutive-trial analysis misleads. Model-free agents that exploit links between reward location and good actions look model-based even under more advanced analyses.
numbers: No participant data. Simulations only; a suggested analysis correction restored power.
limits: Only abstract and author summary read (the full-text download was lost). Exact effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Another reason not to trust a single stay-probability score as proof of planning, in humans or in an LLM.

source: Gillan, Kosinski, Whelan, Phelps, Daw (2016) Characterizing a psychiatric symptom dimension related to deficits in goal-directed control
finding: Individual differences. Model-based learning falls with a compulsive-behaviour and intrusive-thought dimension, not with depression or anxiety scores. Replicated in a second sample.
numbers: Exp 1 N=548: OCD beta=-0.040, SE 0.02, p=0.049 (14% lower model-based learning); depression p=0.439; anxiety p=0.778. Exp 2 N=1413: eating disorders beta=-0.037 (p<0.001), impulsivity -0.034 (p=0.007), OCD -0.026 (p=0.020), alcohol -0.025 (p=0.029), depression -0.010 (p=0.385). Factor contrast vs Anxious-Depression beta=-0.062, p=0.001.
limits: Online general population. Effects small. The instruction-comprehension problem in b09 may inflate between-person differences.
agent_relevance: Planning use varies by person-level trait, so any gate must be calibrated per task and per agent, not set once.

source: Otto, Raio, Chiang, Phelps, Daw (2013) Working-memory capacity protects model-based learning from stress
finding: Moderator: stress. Cold-pressor stress (3 min ice water) and cortisol rise reduced the model-based contribution but not the model-free one. Low working-memory participants were hit; high-span participants were protected.
numbers: N=56 recruited (48 after exclusions); 200 two-step trials; 5 cents per rewarded trial. Cortisol condition-by-time F=19.99, P<0.0001. OSPAN x cortisol x reward x transition interaction P<0.01.
limits: Small N. Working memory as mediator is correlational. Later stress replications have been mixed (not re-checked this session).
agent_relevance: Planning leans on working memory. For an LLM, crowded context may play the same role as stress: keep the planning slot's context clean.

source: Gillan, Otto, Phelps, Daw (2015) Model-based learning protects against forming habits
finding: Linking the two-step task to habit tests. Individual model-based learning predicted later sensitivity to outcome devaluation. Model-free learning did not. So model-based use protects against habit.
numbers: Exp 1 N=90 online. Consumption-sensitivity control: Spearman r=.12, p=.278 (unrelated to devaluation sensitivity). A second independent sample replicated.
limits: Online samples; correlational; devaluation test is a different task from the two-step task.
agent_relevance: Planning use predicts flexibility when goals change. An agent that plans less will adapt more slowly when conditions change.

source: Miller, Shenhav, Ludvig (2019) Habits without values
finding: Rival theory. Habits are modeled as direct strengthening of repeated actions, not as cached values. The model reproduces devaluation and degradation insensitivity and perseveration without a value-based model-free learner.
numbers: Simulations of devaluation, contingency degradation, reinforcement-schedule effects.
limits: Challenges the model-free = habit mapping. The two-system split may not carve habits at the joints.
agent_relevance: A repeated move can be sticky for reasons unrelated to cached value. Add a repetition-bias check beside the value check.

source: Collins & Cockburn (2020) Beyond dichotomies in reinforcement learning
finding: Review arguing the model-based/model-free split is over-used. It blurs working memory, episodic memory and other processes that mimic each system. Questions should be re-aimed at the components.
numbers: Review; no new data.
limits: Opinion paper but widely cited. Agrees with b09, b10, b14.
agent_relevance: Do not wire the schema to a two-system story. Wire it to measurable parts: cost, uncertainty, memory.

source: Momennejad, Otto, Daw, Norman (2018) Offline replay supports planning in human reinforcement learning
finding: Planning need not happen at decision time. Offline replay of trajectories integrates changed rewards with past knowledge, and prediction-error uncertainty triggers replay. Replay evidence predicted later replanning.
numbers: fMRI 2-step revaluation task; abstract-level read, no counts recorded.
limits: Only abstract read. Single-lab fMRI.
agent_relevance: Planning work can move off the critical path: do it between steps and store the result as a cache (compile-then-cache).

source: Smid et al. (2023) Neurocognitive basis of model-based decision making and its metacontrol in childhood
finding: Development as moderator. Children 5 to 11 already show model-based signatures that grow with age, but metacontrol (using planning when it pays) varies widely. Metacontrol relates to an inhibition task and cortical thickness.
numbers: N=69 aged 6 to 13 on a two-step task; N=44 with structural MRI.
limits: Cross-sectional, small. Metacontrol is the weakest-measured part.
agent_relevance: Knowing how to plan and knowing when to plan are separate skills. The second is what S0 needs.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Wang, Schulz (2024) CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
finding: Runs the two-step task as a model-basedness measure on LLMs. 35 models phenotyped. RLHF models sit closer to humans on behavioural metrics. Take-a-step-back prompting fostered model-based behaviour. Chain of thought improved probabilistic reasoning rather than model-basedness.
numbers: 35 LLMs; ten behavioural metrics from seven experiments; model-basedness from a two-step task, normalised so random=0, human=1. Model size and code training did not significantly affect model-basedness.
limits: Prompt effects tested on a few models; the instruction-comprehension issue (b09) applies. Per-model values not extracted.
agent_relevance: First direct LLM measurement of the construct. Prompt shape can move model-based behaviour: test the S0 prompt on it.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: A language model fine-tuned on human choices from many experiments (including the two-step task) simulates human behaviour there. It also captured the magic-carpet version of the Feher da Silva and Hare task, which was not in training.
numbers: Figure compares human and Centaur distributions of reward and of a model-based parameter; held-out magic-carpet prediction reported as negative log-likelihood.
limits: Matches summary distributions, not proof of the same mechanism. Later critiques of Centaur not checked.
agent_relevance: A model can imitate the stay-probability pattern without planning. Do not treat a good score on this task as evidence of planning.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating cognitive maps and planning in large language models with CogEval
finding: Protocol testing cognitive maps and planning on 8 LLMs with prompts built from human planning experiments. Reports planning failures such as invalid paths and trouble finding shortest routes.
numbers: Eight LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, davinci-003, Bard, Cohere, Claude-1, LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B); abstract and opening read, failure counts not extracted.
limits: Older models (2023). Detailed accuracy numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Model-based planning in LLMs was weak in 2023; the planning gain must be measured on the current model.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: LLM analogue of paying planning cost with no gain. o1-like models use many extra tokens on trivial questions; most correct answers appear in the first solution; later solutions add little. Self-training to trim them kept accuracy.
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3?' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. Worked example: first correct solution at 39 of 901 tokens = 4.3% efficiency.
limits: Open o1-like models (QwQ and similar) on math. Trimming used the first correct solution as training signal, which needs a known answer.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that always-plan wastes budget on easy items; supports an S0 gate keyed on difficulty.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: reasoning models can learn when to think
finding: RL teaches a reasoning model to choose Thinking or NoThinking by difficulty. For relatively simple tasks NoThinking is better for both accuracy and efficiency.
numbers: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B across math sets: average response length cut by 53% and accuracy up by 2.4%.
limits: Trained on math sets; one model family; gains modest per set.
agent_relevance: Learned arbitration works but needs training. A scaffold must use cheaper signals.

source: Paglieri et al. (2025) Learning when to plan: efficiently allocating test-time compute for LLM agents
finding: Agent version of the arbitration problem. Always planning is expensive and degrades long-horizon performance; never planning also limits results. Each task has a 'Goldilocks' planning frequency. SFT then RL gave agents that plan when needed and replan rarely, more sample efficient than non-planning baselines.
numbers: Crafter and POGS zero-shot results over 100 seeds; Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned; SFT-primed planners more sample efficient.
limits: Small open model, two game environments; effect sizes given in figures only.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM test of the S0 question: both extremes lose, so a gate must exist and be tuned per task.

source: Ghoshal & Al-Bustami (2026) When do tools and planning help LLMs think? A cost- and latency-aware benchmark
finding: Planning helps in one setting and not in another. On Event-QA the best tool-augmented setup raised accuracy; on CMV one-shot prompting was strongest and planning only added latency.
numbers: GPT-4o Event-QA accuracy 47.5% to 67.5% while latency rose from 8 s to 317 s per example. GPT-4o-mini CMV one-shot 75% at 6 s.
limits: Two tasks, two OpenAI models. Planning stack mixed with retrieval and tools, so planning alone is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Plan benefit depends on task type and the cost can be about 40x latency; gate must be task-conditional.

source: He & Feng (2026) When to think deeply: inhibitory deliberation for LLM reasoning (IDPR)
finding: Fast answer first, then a controller decides whether to release it or call slow reasoning, using the fast answer's confidence, logit margin and cost. Framed after the expected value of control.
numbers: 5,000-example math test: slow reasoning on 8.20% of examples; accuracy 47.90% to 48.92% (about +1.0 point); random routing under the same budget lowers accuracy.
limits: Gain is small in absolute terms. Needs logits, so not for a closed API. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A response-conditioned gate beats random routing at equal cost. Condition the S0 gate on the first answer, not only on the question.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: a generative agent with fast and slow thinking for complex interactive tasks
finding: Dual-module agent. A small fast model acts by imitation; a large LM is called for planning and grounding when a heuristic detects an exception. It beat ReAct, Reflexion and SayCan while using fewer tokens per action.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3.
limits: Hand-written switch rule. One benchmark. Part of the gain is from the imitation-trained fast module.
agent_relevance: Working example of a trigger-based switch from cached to deliberate mode, with rule-based triggers on failure.

source: Decker, Otto, Daw, Hartley (2016) From creatures of habit to goal-directed learners: tracking the developmental emergence of model-based reinforcement learning
finding: Developmental moderator (background knowledge, not opened): model-based signatures in the two-step task rise from childhood to adulthood.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Planning skill builds over time; arbitration may be a learned skill.

source: Dezfouli & Balleine (2013) Actions, action sequences and habits: evidence that goal-directed and habitual action control are hierarchically organized
finding: Rival account (not opened): habits are chunked action sequences, and goal-directed control chooses among sequences. Fits human and rodent data without a value cache.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Cached routines may be chunks of steps; relates to the chunking subfield.
